author: Human
standardized_text:
SCIENTIFIC BACKGROUND AND RESEARCH QUESTION
Plant biology investigates the mechanisms of cytokinesis and its robustness under heat stress. Current knowledge identifies cytokinesis as essential for biomass production while noting that its heat sensitivity varies between temperate and resilient species. This project identifies genetic bottlenecks of cytokinetic robustness to inform evolutionary strategies and the development of heat-resilient crops.

METHODOLOGY AND ANALYTICAL APPROACH
The study employs a systematic comparative bioinformatics analysis of single-cell and whole-organ omics datasets under control and heat-stress conditions. Researchers will apply orthology inference methods and co-expression network analysis to construct multi-layered genetic networks. Results will be validated by selecting transcripts co-expressed with known mitotic genes and filtering for cross-species consistency.

DATA SOURCES AND SYNTHESIS PLAN
The project utilizes publicly available omics datasets for Arabidopsis thaliana, Zea mays, Oryza sativa, Sorghum bicolor, and Nicotiana tabacum. These distinct datasets will be integrated by reprocessing all raw data through a standardized pipeline to normalize variations in growth conditions. Variability in experimental conditions will be mitigated by standardized reprocessing and by aggregating a large volume of datasets to reduce noise.

FEASIBILITY AND TIMELINE
The two-year timeline includes the submission of a network analysis manuscript by the end of the second year followed by a theoretical review article. This project requires a multi-disciplinary working group to combine expertise in plant cell biology and membrane trafficking with professional bioinformatics capabilities.

OPEN SCIENCE AND TEAM COMPOSITION
The team will publish findings as a research manuscript and a review article while sharing all code and data publicly. The team consists of experts in plant cytokinesis and heat stress physiology supported by specialized bioinformatics staff.

criteria.justification: The project targets cytokinesis robustness under heat stress, which can be framed as an emergent, system-level property of interacting molecular networks, but emergence is not explicitly articulated as a central mesoscale concept.

Cross-species integration of heat-stress omics to identify conserved cytokinetic bottlenecks is a meaningful advance, but the proposal reads as an incremental extension of established comparative network approaches rather than a clearly transformative new framework.

The overall logic (orthology + co-expression networks + cross-species consistency) is sound, but key methodological details are missing (batch correction strategy, network inference choices, statistical thresholds, and how 'validation' will be performed without new experiments).

A two-year reprocessing and integration effort across multiple species and modalities is plausible, but heterogeneity in tissues, developmental stages, and heat-stress regimes may substantially slow harmonization and reduce interpretability without clearer milestones and contingencies.
The work is explicitly based on reanalysis and integration of publicly available omics datasets across species, with no new data generation proposed.

Species are listed, but specific repositories/accessions, dataset inclusion criteria, and modality breakdowns are not provided, and limitations are under-addressed (e.g., confounding by tissue/stage, stress intensity/duration, platform effects, and uneven annotation quality across species).

The proposal commits to sharing code and data and publishing outputs, but lacks concrete reproducibility plans (versioned workflows/containers, preregistered analysis plan, governance for team science, and specific repositories/metadata standards).
The proposal addresses mesoscale cellular processes (cytokinesis and genetic networks), but it does not explicitly frame its research questions around 'emergent phenomena' as requested by the call.

Comparing single-cell and whole-organ omics across multiple plant species to identify conserved cytokinetic bottlenecks is an innovative approach with significant potential to inform the development of heat-resilient crops.
The methodology is highly logical and grounded in established bioinformatics practices, utilizing standardized reprocessing, orthology inference, and cross-species filtering to ensure robust results.

While achievable with specialized staff, reprocessing and integrating both single-cell and whole-organ omics data for five distinct species within a two-year timeframe is highly ambitious and presents potential bottleneck challenges.

The proposal explicitly identifies the five plant species to be used and thoughtfully addresses the limitations of experimental variability by proposing standardized reprocessing and large-volume aggregation.

The methodology lacks specificity regarding which orthology inference methods will be used, how co-expression networks will be constructed, and what statistical thresholds will define significance. The validation approach of selecting transcripts co-expressed with known mitotic genes is circular and insufficiently rigorous.

title_norm: emergent immune evasion mechanisms mediated by bulky glycan shields in the glycocalyx
title: Emergent Immune Evasion Mechanisms Mediated by Bulky Glycan Shields in the Glycocalyx
author: gemini-3-pro-preview
abstract_original: This proposal examines the cell surface glycocalyx—a dense, mesoscale forest of sugars—and its emergent property of regulating immune cell access. We hypothesize that the physical height and density of the glycocalyx act as a 'kinetic trap' for immune receptors, an emergent biophysical barrier distinct from chemical recognition. We will synthesize glycomics data, atomic force microscopy measurements of cell surface height, and immune cell adhesion assays. By modeling the steric repulsion and thermodynamic entropy of the polymer brush layer using the synthesized data, we aim to predict immune evasion thresholds. Insights will reveal how cancer cells exploit this emergent physical barrier to evade T-cell attack, offering new perspectives for immunotherapy. This requires a synthesis of glycobiology, polymer physics, and immunology.
full_draft_original:
The cell surface is not a smooth, naked membrane but is coated in a dense, complex array of sugar chains attached to proteins and lipids, known as the glycocalyx. This structure represents a quintessential mesoscale phenomenon, extending anywhere from 10 nm to over 1000 nm from the cell membrane—a scale significantly larger than individual receptors but smaller than cellular organelles. While molecular biology has meticulously cataloged the enzymatic pathways constructing individual glycans (glycosylation), and cell biology has characterized the signaling outcomes of receptor-ligand interactions, a critical gap exists in understanding the emergent physical properties of the glycocalyx as a collective whole. Current paradigms in immunology largely focus on chemical recognition: the 'lock and key' fit between a T-cell receptor (TCR) and a tumor antigen. However, this reductionist view fails to account for the physical reality that these receptors must penetrate a dense 'forest' of bulky glycoproteins (mucins) and proteoglycans to achieve contact. 

Existing literature suggests that cancer cells frequently upregulate bulky glycoproteins like MUC1 and MUC16. While these are often studied as signaling molecules, their collective presence creates a polymer brush layer. Polymer physics dictates that as the density and height of these polymers increase, the entropic cost for a second surface (like an immune cell membrane) to compress this layer increases exponentially. This is an emergent property: the barrier function is not encoded in a single sugar molecule but arises from the collective density, rigidity, and hydration of the entire mesoscale assembly. 

Despite the availability of vast public datasets—including The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) for gene expression, GlyGen and UniCarbKB for glycan structures, and scattered repositories of Atomic Force Microscopy (AFM) data characterizing cell stiffness and topography—these domains remain siloed. Glycobiologists analyze mass spectrometry data; physicists model polymer brushes; immunologists study cytokine release. There has been no concerted effort to synthesize these disparate data types to model the glycocalyx as a biophysical shield. This lack of synthesis obscures a fundamental mechanism of immune evasion: the 'kinetic trap,' where the glycocalyx prevents the close apposition (~15nm) required for immunological synapse formation, rendering the cancer cell invisible to the immune system regardless of antigenicity. By synthesizing transcriptomic predictors of glycocalyx composition with biophysical models of polymer brush behavior, this project will illuminate how mesoscale organization dictates cellular fate, addressing a grand challenge in understanding how molecular parts sum to create functional cellular barriers.

This project models the glycocalyx as a biophysical barrier to determine if its physical properties predict immune evasion in cancer.

title_norm: mitochondrial cristae morphodynamics and the emergence of bioenergetic efficiency
title: Mitochondrial Cristae Morphodynamics and the Emergence of Bioenergetic Efficiency
author: gemini-3-pro-preview
abstract_original: This research addresses how the complex folding of mitochondrial cristae (inner membrane invaginations) leads to the emergent property of enhanced respiration efficiency and supercomplex assembly. The geometry of the cristae at the mesoscale is hypothesized to act as a proton trap, an emergent phenomenon critical for ATP synthesis. We will synthesize electron tomography data of mitochondrial ultrastructure, super-resolution imaging of respiratory chain complexes, and bioenergetic flux data. Our hypothesis is that specific cristae geometries optimize the spatial distance between proton pumps and ATP synthase, creating localized pH gradients (micro-domains) that boost efficiency beyond bulk membrane theory. We will use multiphysics simulations (combining diffusion and electrostatics) on real-world membrane geometries derived from tomography data. Insights will link mesoscale membrane architecture directly to metabolic output, relevant for understanding aging and metabolic diseases. This team science approach needs mitochondrial biologists, image analysis experts, and biophysical modelers.
full_draft_original:
The classical chemiosmotic theory, proposed by Peter Mitchell, describes mitochondrial ATP synthesis as a function of a bulk electrochemical proton gradient across the inner mitochondrial membrane (IMM). While this macroscopic view explains the fundamental driving force of bioenergetics, it fails to account for the observed efficiency and stability of respiration under fluctuating metabolic demands. Recent advances in structural biology suggest that the IMM is not a simple barrier but a highly dynamic, architecturally complex structure characterized by invaginations known as cristae. These cristae are connected to the inner boundary membrane by narrow tubular junctions, creating distinct sub-compartments. At the mesoscale—the critical regime between molecular protein structures and the organelle level—these architectural features likely give rise to emergent phenomena that cannot be predicted by studying isolated respiratory complexes or whole-mitochondria bulk assays.

Current literature indicates that the spatial organization of the Electron Transport Chain (ETC) complexes into 'supercomplexes' (respirasomes) and the geometric curvature of the cristae membrane are tightly coupled. However, a significant gap exists in quantifying how specific mesoscale geometries influence proton diffusion kinetics and local pH gradients. Experimental evidence from cryo-electron tomography (cryo-ET) has provided high-resolution snapshots of mitochondrial ultrastructure, yet these static images have rarely been integrated with kinetic data to model dynamic function. Furthermore, while the Protein Data Bank (PDB) contains near-atomic resolution structures of individual complexes, and the Electron Microscopy Public Image Archive (EMPIAR) holds terabytes of tomographic data, these datasets remain siloed. There is currently no comprehensive synthesis that maps the precise atomic coordinates of pumps into the realistic, biologically variable membrane manifolds found in public repositories to test bioenergetic efficiency.

This synthesis research is timely and significant because it addresses the 'structure-function' gap at the mesoscale. We posit that the cristae act as kinetic proton traps—an emergent property arising from the restriction of diffusion through cristae junctions and the electrostatic focusing of protons along highly curved membrane ridges. Understanding this phenomenon is crucial because the loss of cristae curvature is a hallmark of aging, neurodegeneration, and metabolic disorders. By synthesizing existing structural and bioenergetic data, we can move beyond qualitative descriptions of 'swollen' or 'fragmented' mitochondria to a quantitative, biophysical understanding of how membrane morphodynamics drive energy transduction. This project leverages the NCEMS mission by utilizing vast, under-analyzed public datasets to solve the long-standing puzzle of how mitochondria maintain high thermodynamic efficiency, transforming static structural atlases into dynamic bioenergetic models.

SCIENTIFIC BACKGROUND AND RESEARCH QUESTION
Mitochondrial biology investigates the relationship between mitochondrial cristae geometry and bioenergetic efficiency to address the lack of a quantitative link between membrane architecture and ATP synthesis. Chemiosmotic theory explains bulk electrochemical gradients but fails to account for the efficiency of respiration within complex and dynamic cristae structures. This project determines how cristae geometry influences proton diffusion and respiratory chain organization to resolve the structure-function gap at the mesoscale.

METHODOLOGY AND ANALYTICAL APPROACH
The study employs a Mesoscale Digital Twin approach to synthesize structural and bioenergetic data into dynamic finite-element models of mitochondrial membranes. Researchers utilize cryo-electron tomography processing and AI-driven segmentation alongside finite element analysis and agent-based modeling to construct these simulations. Results undergo in silico cross-validation by comparing simulated ATP production rates against published oxygen consumption data from mutant and wild-type cell lines.

DATA SOURCES AND SYNTHESIS PLAN
The project utilizes datasets from the Electron Microscopy Public Image Archive (EMPIAR) and the Protein Data Bank (PDB) alongside the Electron Microscopy Data Bank (EMDB) and BRENDA. Investigators integrate these distinct sources by mapping atomic coordinates of respiratory complexes onto three-dimensional membrane meshes derived from tomographic data. Automated segmentation pipelines and data harmonization mitigate the challenges of data heterogeneity and siloing to ensure consistent model construction.

FEASIBILITY AND TIMELINE
The three-year timeline allocates the first year to data mining and segmentation before proceeding to model construction and final validation. This project requires cross-disciplinary collaboration to bridge the disparate expertise of structural biology and biophysics and data science.

OPEN SCIENCE AND TEAM COMPOSITION
The team will release an open-access Mito-Mesoscale Atlas and an open-source simulation pipeline on GitHub and Zenodo while hosting a modeling workshop. The interdisciplinary team includes a structural biologist and a computational biophysicist and a data scientist alongside a graduate student researcher.

standardized_text:
SCIENTIFIC BACKGROUND AND RESEARCH QUESTION
This project investigates mammalian hibernation physiology to identify the molecular mechanisms that facilitate metabolic suppression and tissue preservation. Current research relies on single-species studies that fail to account for phylogenetic relationships when analyzing transcriptional variation across diverse hibernating mammals. The study identifies conserved molecular processes to reveal fundamental mechanisms of metabolic modulation that inform human health applications like ischemia tolerance.

METHODOLOGY AND ANALYTICAL APPROACH
The study design utilizes a comparative and phylogenetically informed analysis of existing RNA-seq datasets through longitudinal state comparisons. Key methods include RNA-seq read mapping with STAR and the application of Ornstein-Uhlenbeck processes to model gene expression evolution. Results are validated through simulation tests and Gene Ontology (GO) and KEGG pathway overrepresentation analyses.

DATA SOURCES AND SYNTHESIS PLAN
The project utilizes publicly available RNA-seq data from the NCBI Short Read Archive alongside reference genomes and whole-genome alignments. Datasets are integrated by mapping raw reads to reference genomes and establishing orthology across species to harmonize metadata. Known limitations regarding sparse sampling and variable data quality are mitigated through rigorous quality control and phylogenetic models designed for missing data.

FEASIBILITY AND TIMELINE
The project follows a 24-month timeline that begins with data processing and concludes with the dissemination of findings. This scope requires cross-disciplinary collaboration to integrate diverse omics data types and manage high-dimensional computational challenges.

OPEN SCIENCE AND TEAM COMPOSITION
The project commits to open science by publishing a curated dataset and developing new analytical tools for public use. The team consists of a multidisciplinary group of specialists in cell physiology and genomics supported by staff scientists focused on technical execution.

SCIENTIFIC BACKGROUND AND RESEARCH QUESTION
Protein structural biology investigates the evolutionary origins and functional consequences of complex protein topologies like knots and pierced lassos. Current research lacks a method to identify the specific phylogenetic branch points where these nontrivial topological changes occur within protein families. This study identifies evolutionary turning points of topological changes to determine how entanglements correlate with functional and adaptive characteristics.

METHODOLOGY AND ANALYTICAL APPROACH
The study design employs a comparative evolutionary analysis that integrates sequence and structural data to map the emergence of entangled topologies. The approach utilizes phylogenetic reconstruction and structural bioinformatics tools including KnotProt and AlphaKnot to annotate and model protein structures. Results are validated through statistical analysis of structural features and comparisons with known functional hotspots and thermal stability data.

DATA SOURCES AND SYNTHESIS PLAN
The project utilizes diverse databases including UniProt and the Protein Data Bank (PDB) alongside AlphaFold DB and the Meltome Atlas. Researchers integrate these datasets by overlaying functional and topological annotations onto reconstructed phylogenetic trees to identify statistically significant evolutionary patterns. Limited structural information at specific branch points is mitigated by generating new structural models with GPU-intensive prediction tools.

FEASIBILITY AND TIMELINE
The project follows a 24-month timeline that progresses from initial data gathering to phylogenetic tree generation and final publication of findings. This scope requires cross-disciplinary collaboration between experts in evolutionary analysis and database management to synthesize these complex and diverse datasets.

OPEN SCIENCE AND TEAM COMPOSITION
The project provides an open data-driven platform and publishes all findings in peer-reviewed literature to ensure public access. The team includes experts in evolutionary analysis and structural biology who support a Staff Scientist and an Assistant for computational tasks.

The overall workflow is logical (phylogenies + topology annotation + functional overlays), but key methodological details are missing (orthology definition, tree uncertainty handling, topology-calling error rates, and statistical controls for phylogenetic non-independence).

A 24-month plan is plausible, but the scope is broad and feasibility depends on substantial compute and careful curation; the proposal lacks concrete milestones, contingencies, and criteria for narrowing to tractable protein families.

The project is largely integrative across UniProt/PDB/AlphaFold/Meltome/KnotProt, but the plan to generate new structural models with GPU-intensive prediction tools risks drifting toward new data generation rather than strict synthesis of existing public resources.

Major data sources are clearly named and the proposal acknowledges sparse structural coverage at key branch points, though it under-discusses limitations such as AlphaFold confidence for knotted regions, PDB sampling bias, and topology-annotation false positives/negatives.

title_norm: lipid raft dynamics and the emergence of signal fidelity during t-cell activation
title: Lipid Raft Dynamics and the Emergence of Signal Fidelity During T-Cell Activation
author: gemini-3-pro-preview
abstract_original: This proposal examines the emergent role of lipid rafts (mesoscale membrane nanodomains) in generating high-fidelity signaling thresholds in immune cells. T-cell receptor (TCR) triggering exhibits remarkable sensitivity and specificity, an emergent property that cannot be explained by simple ligand-receptor binding affinity. We will synthesize lipidomics datasets, single-molecule tracking data of TCR dynamics from the biological literature, and super-resolution microscopy data (STORM/PALM) available in the BioImage Archive. The central question is how the dynamic clustering of specific lipids (cholesterol, sphingolipids) and proteins creates a mesoscale 'computational engine' that filters noise and amplifies true antigenic signals. We will employ agent-based modeling and molecular dynamics simulations (coarse-grained) to integrate lipid composition data with protein mobility tracks. We expect to demonstrate that lipid rafts function as emergent signal integration hubs that undergo phase transitions to lock in activation states, providing a physical basis for immune decision-making. This synthesis requires a collaborative effort between immunologists, membrane biophysicists, and computational modelers to link compositional lipid data with spatiotemporal signaling outcomes.
full_draft_original:
The molecular mechanism by which T-cells discriminate between self and non-self antigens remains one of the most enduring puzzles in immunology. While the biochemical interactions between the T-cell receptor (TCR) and peptide-MHC complexes are well-characterized at the atomic scale, these interactions alone fail to explain the extraordinary fidelity of the immune response. T-cells can detect a handful of agonist ligands amidst a sea of thousands of endogenous self-peptides, a phenomenon that implies an emergent property arising not from individual molecules, but from their collective organization at the mesoscale. Current paradigms, such as kinetic proofreading and serial triggering, provide partial explanations but often neglect the active role of the plasma membrane environment. Specifically, the dynamic heterogeneity of the membrane—often described as 'lipid rafts' or membrane nanodomains—represents a critical mesoscale layer that organizes the signaling machinery in space and time.

Lipid rafts are sterol- and sphingolipid-enriched nanodomains (10-200 nm) that compartmentalize cellular processes. Despite decades of study, the functional role of these domains in TCR signaling remains controversial, largely because experimental data is fragmented across disciplines. Immunologists have generated vast amounts of flow cytometry and functional signaling data; biophysicists have produced high-resolution single-molecule tracking (SMT) and super-resolution microscopy (STORM/PALM/STED) datasets detailing protein diffusion; and lipid biochemists have cataloged membrane compositions via mass spectrometry-based lipidomics. However, these datasets remain siloed. We lack a unified framework that connects the chemical composition of the membrane (lipidomics) with the spatiotemporal behavior of receptors (microscopy) to explain the binary outcome of T-cell activation (immunology).

This synthesis project addresses a specific gap: the lack of a mesoscale model that integrates lipid composition with protein dynamics to explain signal discrimination. We posit that the 'decision' to activate is an emergent phase transition driven by the coalescence of lipid nanodomains, acting as a noise filter. Existing data is now sufficient to test this. The proliferation of super-resolution data in repositories like the BioImage Archive and the accumulation of quantitative lipidomics in the LIPID MAPS Structure Database provide the raw material to construct a 'virtual membrane.' By synthesizing these disparate data sources, we can move beyond static snapshots of membrane organization to understand the dynamic, emergent behavior of the immunological synapse. This research is significant because it shifts the focus from 'lock-and-key' molecular binding to 'dynamic clustering' as the primary driver of signal fidelity, offering new insights into how biological systems manage signal-to-noise ratios at the mesoscale.

title_norm: integration of structural and immunopeptidomic data for modeling emergent antigen processing in the immunoproteasome
title: Integration of Structural and Immunopeptidomic Data for Modeling Emergent Antigen Processing in the Immunoproteasome
author: claude-opus-4-5
abstract_original: The immunoproteasome generates MHC-presented peptides through emergent cleavage patterns that differ from constitutive proteasomes—a mesoscale phenomenon where subunit composition alters processing outcomes. This synthesis project will decode how immunoproteasome assembly creates emergent epitope generation by integrating structural biology and immunopeptidomics. We will synthesize cryo-EM structures from EMDB of proteasome variants, immunopeptidomic data from IEDB and SysteMHC Atlas, protein sequence data from UniProt, and transcriptomics correlating proteasome subunit expression with peptide repertoires. The central question is: how does immunoproteasome subunit incorporation create emergent cleavage specificities at the mesoscale (the ~15 nm proteasome barrel) that individual catalytic subunits cannot produce? We hypothesize that emergent cleavage patterns arise from allosteric communication between subunits, altered substrate threading, and cooperative effects among catalytic sites that depend on mesoscale proteasome architecture. Our computational approach combines structural modeling of substrate processing through proteasome channels, machine learning to predict cleavage sites from sequence and proteasome composition, and network analysis of epitope generation pathways. We will develop algorithms correlating proteasome subunit expression patterns with immunopeptidome composition across cell types. Integration with T cell epitope databases will connect emergent cleavage to immune recognition. Analysis across disease states (cancer, infection, autoimmunity) will reveal how altered proteasome composition shifts emergent epitope generation. The synthesis of structural, immunopeptidomic, and expression data exceeds single-lab scope. Expected outcomes include predictive models of emergent epitope generation, identification of key subunit interactions governing cleavage specificity, and principles for modulating antigen processing. Understanding emergent immunoproteasome function has implications for vaccine design and cancer immunotherapy. All predictive models, analysis pipelines, and curated datasets will be openly released.
full_draft_original:
The proteasome represents one of the most sophisticated molecular machines in eukaryotic cells, serving as the primary engine of intracellular protein degradation. This ~2.5 MDa barrel-shaped complex, spanning approximately 15 nm in length and 11 nm in diameter, occupies a critical position at the mesoscale—the organizational level between individual biomolecules and membrane-bound organelles. The constitutive proteasome (c20S) contains three catalytic β-subunits (β1, β2, β5) that provide caspase-like, trypsin-like, and chymotrypsin-like activities, respectively. Upon interferon-γ stimulation or during immune cell development, these subunits are replaced by immunoproteasome-specific variants (β1i/LMP2, β2i/MECL-1, β5i/LMP7), fundamentally altering the peptide products generated.

Critically, the immunoproteasome does not simply produce more peptides—it generates qualitatively different peptide repertoires with distinct C-terminal residues, lengths, and sequences that preferentially bind MHC class I molecules. This represents a quintessential emergent phenomenon: the whole-complex behavior cannot be predicted from the properties of individual subunits. Each immunosubunit, when studied in isolation or in hybrid proteasomes, exhibits different cleavage preferences than when all three immunosubunits are incorporated together. This emergent specificity arises from the mesoscale architecture of the assembled proteasome barrel, where allosteric communication between catalytic chambers, substrate threading through the central channel, and cooperative interactions among active sites create processing outcomes that transcend individual subunit properties.

Existing literature has established several key observations that remain mechanistically unexplained. Structural studies deposited in the Electron Microscopy Data Bank (EMDB) reveal subtle but significant conformational differences between constitutive and immunoproteasomes, including altered gate dynamics and chamber geometries. Immunopeptidomic studies catalogued in the Immune Epitope Database (IEDB) and SysteMHC Atlas demonstrate that immunoproteasome-expressing cells present distinct peptide repertoires, with enrichment for peptides bearing hydrophobic and basic C-termini. Transcriptomic analyses in Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) show that proteasome subunit expression varies dramatically across cell types, developmental stages, and disease states. However, no systematic synthesis has connected these structural, functional, and expression-level observations to explain how mesoscale proteasome architecture creates emergent cleavage specificity.

Several critical gaps persist in our understanding. First, while individual cryo-EM structures exist for various proteasome configurations, no comprehensive analysis has mapped how structural variations correlate with functional outcomes across the full spectrum of proteasome compositions. Second, immunopeptidomic datasets have been generated independently across laboratories using different cell types, MHC alleles, and analytical methods, but systematic integration to identify proteasome-dependent signatures remains lacking. Third, the relationship between proteasome subunit expression patterns (captured in single-cell RNA-seq datasets from Human Cell Atlas and other consortia) and resulting immunopeptidome composition has not been computationally modeled at scale.

This synthesis project addresses these gaps by integrating heterogeneous public datasets spanning structural biology, immunopeptidomics, and transcriptomics. The mesoscale focus is essential because emergent cleavage properties arise specifically from the assembled proteasome architecture—the spatial arrangement of catalytic sites within the barrel, the dynamics of substrate entry and threading, and the allosteric networks connecting distant regions of the complex. Understanding these emergent properties has profound implications for immunology and medicine. Vaccine design depends on predicting which peptides will be generated and presented; cancer immunotherapy efficacy correlates with tumor immunopeptidome composition; autoimmune diseases involve aberrant self-peptide presentation. By decoding the rules governing emergent epitope generation, this project will provide foundational knowledge enabling rational manipulation of antigen processing for therapeutic benefit.

The timing for this synthesis is optimal. The past decade has witnessed exponential growth in relevant public data: over 50 high-resolution proteasome structures in EMDB/PDB, hundreds of thousands of validated epitopes in IEDB, comprehensive immunopeptidomic atlases in SysteMHC, and millions of single-cell transcriptomes capturing proteasome expression heterogeneity. No single laboratory possesses the expertise to integrate these diverse data types—this challenge demands the transdisciplinary collaboration that NCEMS is uniquely positioned to support.

title_norm: integration of structural and transport data for modeling crm1-mediated cargo recognition in nuclear export
title: Integration of Structural and Transport Data for Modeling CRM1-Mediated Cargo Recognition in Nuclear Export
author: claude-opus-4-5
abstract_original: CRM1-mediated nuclear export achieves selective transport of hundreds of cargoes through a single receptor—emergent selectivity arising from mesoscale complex assembly rather than simple binary interactions. This synthesis project will decode emergent export selectivity by integrating structural biology, proteomics, and transport kinetics. We will synthesize structural data from PDB on CRM1-cargo complexes, nuclear export signal (NES) sequences from NESdb and ValidNES, proteomics of nuclear/cytoplasmic distribution from the Human Protein Atlas, and transport kinetics from published single-molecule studies. The central question is: how does CRM1 achieve emergent selectivity for diverse cargoes through mesoscale ternary complex formation with RanGTP that binary CRM1-cargo interactions cannot explain? We hypothesize that emergent selectivity arises from conformational selection, where RanGTP binding creates allosteric changes in CRM1 that differentially stabilize cargo complexes based on NES properties beyond simple affinity. Our computational approach combines molecular dynamics simulations of CRM1-RanGTP-cargo assemblies, machine learning to predict export efficiency from NES sequence and structure, and kinetic modeling of transport incorporating complex assembly dynamics. We will develop algorithms correlating NES features with export kinetics, identifying sequence and structural determinants of emergent selectivity. Integration with disease mutation data will connect disrupted export to pathological phenotypes. Comparative analysis across CRM1 cargoes will reveal shared versus cargo-specific emergent recognition mechanisms. This project requires expertise in nuclear transport, structural biology, computational chemistry, and proteomics—necessitating collaboration across specialized laboratories. The synthesis of structural, sequence, localization, and kinetic data exceeds single-lab capabilities. Expected outcomes include predictive models of emergent export selectivity, identification of key features determining cargo recognition, and principles for modulating nuclear export. Understanding emergent transport selectivity has implications for diseases involving mislocalized proteins. All models, analysis pipelines, and curated datasets will be openly released.
full_draft_original:
Nuclear transport represents one of the most fundamental processes in eukaryotic cell biology, governing the spatial distribution of proteins between the nucleus and cytoplasm. At the heart of this process lies CRM1 (Chromosome Region Maintenance 1, also known as Exportin-1 or XPO1), the primary nuclear export receptor responsible for transporting over 1,000 distinct protein cargoes across the nuclear envelope. This remarkable feat of selective transport—where a single receptor discriminates among hundreds of substrates with varying affinities and kinetics—exemplifies emergent selectivity at the mesoscale, a phenomenon that cannot be explained by simple binary molecular interactions alone.

The mesoscale regime, spanning approximately 10-100 nanometers between individual biomolecules and organelles, represents a critical frontier in molecular and cellular biology. At this scale, emergent properties arise from the dynamic assembly of multi-component complexes, where the collective behavior of the system transcends the sum of individual molecular interactions. CRM1-mediated export operates precisely at this mesoscale: the functional export complex comprises CRM1 (~120 kDa), the small GTPase RanGTP (~25 kDa), and cargo proteins of varying sizes, forming transient assemblies of 150-500 kDa that must navigate the ~40 nm central channel of the nuclear pore complex (NPC).

Current understanding of CRM1-cargo recognition centers on the nuclear export signal (NES), a short leucine-rich sequence motif typically 10-15 residues in length. Structural studies deposited in the Protein Data Bank (PDB) have revealed that NES peptides bind to a hydrophobic groove on CRM1's outer convex surface. The consensus NES pattern (Φ-X2-3-Φ-X2-3-Φ-X-Φ, where Φ represents hydrophobic residues) has been catalogued in databases such as NESdb and ValidNES, which collectively document over 250 experimentally validated NES sequences. However, this binary view of CRM1-NES recognition fails to explain several critical observations.

First, NES sequences exhibit remarkable diversity, with binding affinities spanning four orders of magnitude (Kd from nanomolar to hundreds of micromolar), yet many weak-binding cargoes are efficiently exported. Second, RanGTP binding to CRM1 is essential for cargo loading, but the mechanistic basis for this cooperativity remains incompletely understood. Structural data reveal that RanGTP binding induces conformational changes in CRM1, transitioning from a compact, autoinhibited state to an extended, cargo-receptive conformation. This allosteric coupling suggests that emergent selectivity arises not from static NES-CRM1 affinity but from the dynamic interplay within the ternary CRM1-RanGTP-cargo complex.

Third, subcellular localization data from the Human Protein Atlas reveal that proteins with similar NES sequences can exhibit dramatically different nuclear/cytoplasmic distributions, indicating that factors beyond NES affinity determine export efficiency. Single-molecule studies of nuclear transport, while limited in number, have documented cargo-specific transport kinetics that do not correlate simply with measured binding affinities.

These observations point to a fundamental gap in our understanding: the emergent selectivity of CRM1-mediated export arises from mesoscale complex assembly dynamics that cannot be predicted from binary interaction data alone. This gap is precisely suited for synthesis research because the relevant data exist across multiple domains—structural biology, sequence databases, proteomics, and transport kinetics—but have never been systematically integrated to address this question.

The significance of understanding emergent export selectivity extends beyond basic biology. Dysregulated nuclear export is implicated in numerous diseases, including cancer, where CRM1 overexpression drives cytoplasmic mislocalization of tumor suppressors such as p53, BRCA1, and APC. The CRM1 inhibitor Selinexor (KPT-330) has received FDA approval for multiple myeloma and diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, yet patient responses vary considerably, likely reflecting cargo-specific effects that current models cannot predict. Disease mutation databases such as ClinVar and COSMIC contain thousands of variants in CRM1 cargoes, many affecting NES regions, whose functional consequences remain unpredictable.

This synthesis project will leverage the unprecedented wealth of publicly available structural, sequence, localization, and kinetic data to decode the principles of emergent export selectivity. By integrating heterogeneous datasets that individually provide only partial views, we will construct comprehensive models that capture the mesoscale dynamics underlying selective nuclear export. This endeavor requires transdisciplinary collaboration spanning nuclear transport biology, structural bioinformatics, computational chemistry, machine learning, and systems biology—expertise distributed across multiple laboratories that must be united to achieve synthesis at the community scale.

abstract_original: Selective autophagy achieves remarkable cargo specificity through receptor proteins that bridge substrates to autophagosomes—an emergent property arising from multivalent interactions at the mesoscale. This synthesis project will decode how autophagy receptors create emergent selectivity by integrating structural biology, proteomics, and cell biology datasets. We will synthesize structural data from PDB on receptor-cargo and receptor-LC3 complexes, autophagy interactomes from BioGRID and published studies, ubiquitin-modified proteomics from PhosphoSitePlus, organelle proteomics from the Human Protein Atlas, and autophagy flux measurements from published screens. The central question is: how do autophagy receptors create emergent selectivity at the mesoscale (10-1000 nm cargo structures) through avidity effects, coincidence detection, and cooperative binding that individual receptor-cargo interactions cannot achieve? We hypothesize that emergent selectivity arises from receptor oligomerization, multivalent cargo recognition, and phase separation creating receptor condensates that amplify weak individual interactions. Our computational approach combines structural modeling of receptor-cargo assemblies, network analysis of autophagy interactomes, and machine learning to predict cargo selectivity from receptor and cargo features. We will develop coarse-grained simulations of receptor clustering on cargo surfaces, testing how avidity emerges from receptor density and cargo geometry. Integration with disease mutation data will connect disrupted receptor-cargo recognition to pathological cargo accumulation. Comparative analysis across selective autophagy pathways (mitophagy, aggrephagy, xenophagy) will reveal shared versus pathway-specific emergent selectivity mechanisms. This project requires expertise in autophagy biology, structural biology, computational modeling, and proteomics—necessitating collaboration across specialized laboratories. The synthesis of structural, proteomic, and phenotypic data across autophagy pathways exceeds single-lab capabilities. Expected outcomes include mechanistic models of emergent selectivity, identification of key features determining cargo recognition, and principles for engineering selective autophagy. Selective autophagy represents one of the most sophisticated quality control mechanisms in eukaryotic cells, enabling the targeted degradation of specific cellular components including damaged organelles, protein aggregates, and invading pathogens. Unlike bulk autophagy, which non-selectively engulfs cytoplasmic material during nutrient starvation, selective autophagy achieves remarkable specificity through a family of receptor proteins that recognize cargo and simultaneously bind to LC3/GABARAP proteins on the autophagosomal membrane. This selectivity is not merely a molecular recognition problem—it represents a quintessential emergent phenomenon at the mesoscale, where the collective behavior of multiple receptor-cargo interactions produces specificity that cannot be predicted from individual binding affinities alone.

The mesoscale regime of selective autophagy spans approximately 10-1000 nanometers, encompassing structures from ubiquitinated protein aggregates to entire mitochondria. At this scale, autophagy receptors such as p62/SQSTM1, NBR1, OPTN, NDP52, and TAX1BP1 must distinguish between substrates that share common molecular features (particularly ubiquitin chains) yet require dramatically different cellular fates. Individual receptor-cargo interactions typically exhibit micromolar affinities—far too weak to explain the observed selectivity and efficiency of cargo capture. This paradox points to emergent selectivity mechanisms operating at the mesoscale.

Recent structural and biochemical studies have revealed that autophagy receptors possess multiple functional domains enabling oligomerization, phase separation, and multivalent cargo engagement. The Protein Data Bank (PDB) now contains over 200 structures of autophagy receptors and their complexes, revealing the molecular basis of LC3-interacting regions (LIRs), ubiquitin-binding domains, and oligomerization interfaces. Cryo-electron microscopy studies have visualized receptor assemblies on cargo surfaces, while mass spectrometry-based proteomics has mapped the autophagy interactome with unprecedented depth. The BioGRID database contains over 3,000 protein-protein interactions involving core autophagy machinery, and PhosphoSitePlus documents thousands of ubiquitination sites on potential autophagy substrates.

Despite this wealth of data, fundamental questions about emergent selectivity remain unanswered. How do receptors with overlapping cargo specificities achieve pathway-specific outcomes? What determines the threshold of ubiquitin density required for cargo recognition? How does receptor oligomerization amplify weak individual interactions into robust cargo capture? These questions cannot be addressed by examining individual receptor-cargo pairs in isolation—they require synthesis across structural, proteomic, and functional datasets to reveal the collective principles governing mesoscale selectivity.

Existing data sources provide unprecedented opportunities for synthesis research. The Human Protein Atlas contains subcellular localization data for autophagy receptors and their cargoes across multiple cell types. Published genome-wide CRISPR screens have identified genetic modifiers of autophagy flux for hundreds of cargo types. Disease mutation databases including ClinVar and COSMIC document pathogenic variants in autophagy receptors associated with neurodegeneration, cancer, and infectious disease susceptibility. The integration of these heterogeneous datasets—spanning molecular structures to cellular phenotypes—exceeds the capabilities of any single laboratory and requires the collaborative, transdisciplinary approach that NCEMS enables.

The significance of understanding emergent selectivity extends beyond basic biology. Defective selective autophagy underlies numerous human diseases, from Parkinson's disease (impaired mitophagy) to inflammatory disorders (defective xenophagy). Therapeutic strategies targeting selective autophagy require mechanistic understanding of how receptors achieve cargo specificity. By synthesizing existing data to decode the principles of emergent selectivity, this project will provide the conceptual foundation for rational manipulation of autophagy pathways. Furthermore, the computational frameworks developed here will establish paradigms for understanding emergent selectivity in other mesoscale biological systems, from immune receptor signaling to membrane trafficking.

title: Decoding Signaling Fidelity through Integrated Phosphoproteomics and Structural Analysis of Kinase-Substrate Networks

abstract_original: Cellular signaling networks achieve remarkable specificity despite kinases sharing similar catalytic mechanisms—an emergent property arising from mesoscale organization including scaffolds, localization, and temporal dynamics. This synthesis project will decode how emergent specificity arises by integrating phosphoproteomics, structural biology, and cell biology datasets. We will synthesize phosphoproteomic data from PhosphoSitePlus and PRIDE (>300,000 phosphosites), kinase-substrate relationships from PhosphoSitePlus and KinaseNET, structural data from PDB on kinase-substrate complexes, protein localization from the Human Protein Atlas, and protein-protein interactions from BioGRID and STRING. The central hypothesis is that signaling specificity emerges from mesoscale organizational features—scaffold-mediated co-localization, compartmentalization, and kinetic proofreading networks—rather than intrinsic kinase-substrate affinity alone. We will develop computational frameworks integrating sequence-based kinase specificity predictions with spatial and temporal context. Machine learning models will predict phosphorylation events by combining kinase motif recognition with localization overlap, scaffold interactions, and network topology. We will construct dynamic models of signaling cascades incorporating mesoscale organization, testing whether emergent specificity requires spatial constraints. Analysis of phosphoproteomic time-series data will reveal how temporal ordering creates emergent pathway specificity. Integration with disease mutation data from COSMIC and ClinVar will identify how disrupted mesoscale organization causes aberrant signaling. Cross-species comparative analysis will distinguish conserved emergent specificity mechanisms from species-specific adaptations. This project requires collaboration between signaling biologists, structural biologists, computational modelers, and data scientists—expertise distributed across institutions. The synthesis of structural, proteomic, localization, and interaction data at proteome scale exceeds single-lab capabilities. Expected outcomes include quantitative models of emergent signaling specificity, identification of key organizational features enabling fidelity, and principles for predicting signaling outcomes. All predictive models, analysis pipelines, and integrated datasets will be openly released, enabling rational intervention in signaling pathways.

The human kinome comprises approximately 538 protein kinases that collectively regulate nearly every cellular process through phosphorylation of over 100,000 documented phosphosites. A fundamental paradox exists at the heart of cellular signaling: kinases with highly similar catalytic domains and overlapping substrate motif preferences nonetheless achieve exquisite specificity in vivo. For example, the AGC kinase family members PKA, PKB/Akt, and PKC share nearly identical phosphorylation consensus motifs (R-X-X-S/T), yet they regulate distinct cellular outcomes including metabolism, survival, and proliferation. This specificity paradox represents a quintessential emergent phenomenon—signaling fidelity arises not from molecular recognition alone but from mesoscale organizational features that operate between the scale of individual protein-protein interactions and cellular compartments.

Current understanding of kinase specificity has been shaped by decades of biochemical and structural studies focusing on intrinsic molecular recognition. Crystal structures deposited in the Protein Data Bank (PDB) have revealed how kinase active sites recognize substrate sequences, with over 500 kinase-substrate complex structures now available. Phosphoproteomic studies catalogued in PhosphoSitePlus and the PRIDE repository have mapped the phosphoproteome across hundreds of cell types and conditions, documenting context-dependent phosphorylation patterns that cannot be explained by sequence motifs alone. Studies from the Human Protein Atlas have revealed that kinases and substrates often occupy distinct subcellular compartments, suggesting that spatial organization constrains signaling outcomes. Protein-protein interaction databases including BioGRID and STRING document extensive scaffold-mediated interactions that bring kinases and substrates into proximity.

Despite this wealth of data, critical gaps remain in our understanding of how mesoscale organization generates emergent specificity. First, existing kinase-substrate prediction algorithms rely predominantly on sequence features and achieve only 60-70% accuracy, failing to capture the organizational context that determines in vivo phosphorylation. Second, while individual studies have demonstrated roles for scaffolds, localization, and temporal dynamics, no systematic framework integrates these features to explain specificity at the proteome scale. Third, the relationship between mesoscale organization and disease-associated signaling dysfunction remains poorly characterized, despite extensive mutation data in COSMIC and ClinVar.

The mesoscale—spanning approximately 10-1000 nanometers—represents the critical organizational level where emergent specificity arises. At this scale, scaffold proteins assemble signaling complexes that increase local kinase-substrate concentrations by orders of magnitude. Membrane microdomains and phase-separated condensates create compartments that restrict kinase access to specific substrate pools. Kinetic proofreading networks, where sequential phosphorylation events create temporal gates, operate through mesoscale assemblies. These organizational features collectively transform promiscuous molecular recognition into precise cellular responses.

Existing publicly available data now enable unprecedented synthesis to decode emergent specificity. PhosphoSitePlus contains over 300,000 non-redundant phosphosites with associated kinase annotations, while PRIDE archives thousands of phosphoproteomic datasets including time-series experiments capturing signaling dynamics. The Human Protein Atlas provides subcellular localization for over 12,000 proteins including most kinases and phosphatases. BioGRID documents over 1.9 million protein interactions including scaffold-mediated complexes. The PDB contains structural information for kinase-substrate recognition. Integration of these resources—beyond the capability of any single laboratory—can reveal how mesoscale features collectively generate emergent specificity.

This synthesis research addresses fundamental questions about biological organization: How do cells achieve reliable information processing using inherently promiscuous molecular components? What organizational principles enable specificity to emerge from molecular chaos? Understanding emergent signaling specificity has profound implications for drug development, as therapeutic kinase inhibitors often produce unexpected effects by disrupting mesoscale organization rather than catalytic activity alone. By synthesizing existing data through collaborative, transdisciplinary analysis, this project will establish quantitative principles governing emergent specificity in cellular signaling.
